text: Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame." All provinces collect a bad harvest. Population stays at three hundred million, so read the x3 row, bad-harvest column. Nobody draws a disaster. Silke, my five's due at the end of the year, same as always.

Graham reads Bad Harvest: a bad harvest for every province, no disasters, the population holds at 300 million (x3). This year's incomes: Silke -30, Reina -30, Paddy -10, Graham +30. The harvest isn't paid out yet. A payment that would take a player below zero is covered first by selling realia on the board back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each, the player choosing which; only the shortfall left becomes a debt.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Another rotten year, and the crown has no shelf left to sell. You all know I put every grain into your fields. Graham, lend the crown thirty now and I'll pay you back thirty-five from the first tax I raise, with your five on top as always. A crown in debt can't pay its share of a single square next year, and that hurts every one of you, not just me. Reina, Paddy: if you have to sell, sell the pieces you need least. The Vase and the Jar are the last things I'd let go to the Pile.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Graham, you're the only granary at this table, so I'll be plain. The Pile pays two for the only Vase in China, and I won't hand it over for two. Twenty-nine buys it outright, or lend me twenty-nine and keep it as your pledge. Either way the Vase stays out of Paddy's hands, and that's worth more to you than whatever Silke's paying in interest. Silke, I'm not selling my land to save a piece. I'll be here next year to pay my share of the square.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Graham, I'll be straight with you, same as I was over the Customs House. I'm five and a half short, and the Pile would take three of my pieces for it. You paid thirteen for the last Brush, so this one's yours for six, right now, and nobody owes anybody. Reina, I'm sorry, I did say it'd be on the shelf for you, but you've one grain and I've a set to keep. If you'd sooner lend me six, Graham, I'll pay it back from the first harvest the new fields bring in, every grain.

Paddy's Bamboo Brush is unsold stock beside the board, and unsold stock is sold only at auction, never privately; it goes up this year at 2. His other offer, a loan of 6, stands. Pieces on the board may be traded at any time.
Not everyone else ends this year in debt: Paddy can cover his 10 by selling his three pieces back (6), ending at 0.5. Without help, Silke would end at -30 and Reina at -25.

Paddy, I won't lend you six. I'll give you ten for the Jar, today. You end the year with grain, you keep your Customs House and your Scroll, and I'm the one who stood aside for that Customs House when it counted. Silke, Reina, I'm sorry. I can do one thing this year and I've picked it.
Graham declines Silke's loan and Reina's Vase, and offers Paddy 10 for the Dragon Jar instead of a loan.

Done, Graham. Ten for the Jar, and I'll shake on it. It's not what it cost me, but you stood aside for me once and you're the only one who's put grain on the table today, so I won't haggle with a man for that. Look after it on Q18. If I ever come asking for it back, I'll be paying properly.

Graham pays Paddy 10 for the Dragon Jar, which moves from R22 to Q18: Graham's set is complete. Reina sells the Vase and the Land Deed Scroll back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each. The harvest is paid: Silke -30, Reina -30, Paddy -10, Graham +30. Grain now: Silke -30 (in debt), Reina -25 (in debt), Paddy 4.5, Graham 52.5.

The set's complete, so I'll use it. Reina, I'm taking the Silk seat. Your twenty-five of debt comes off my grain, not yours, and you start over with sixty and four squares of good wheat land that pay fifty-five a year. Silke, I'm one step closer to you now. I'll be watching the coast.

Graham replaces Reina as the Silk Peasant (Province 5). He takes her -25 with the seat, leaving him 27.5. The Dragon Jar goes back to Province 5's stock, to be auctioned; his Customs House, Bowl and Brush move to P22, P23 and P21. Reina draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and becomes the Wheat Peasant, with Province 7 (the Reservoir and four squares). Graham keeps the bank and the I Ching. Grain: Silke -30 (the crown, in debt), Reina 60, Paddy 4.5, Graham 27.5.

The crown is in debt (-30). Tax collected pays the debt first. While the crown's grain is below zero it can't pay a share of any work or of any square, so no work can be built and no province can buy new land; once it is at 0 or above, it can again. Graham's salary this year is the Emperor's choice; paying it while in debt deepens the debt. The tax may be set anywhere from 10% to 90%.

Ninety percent, and I won't pretend that's gentle. Reina, you're the only one with a harvest to tax, so it comes out of your thirty: twenty-seven grain, and every grain of it pays off the crown's debt, none of it goes on palaces. It still leaves the crown three short. While I'm in the red I can't pay a share of anyone's field, so the fastest way back to land for all of us is to get me out of debt this year, not in three. Graham, your five waits until I'm back above zero. You could have spared me thirty today and picked a seat instead, so you'll understand. Reina, when the crown can pay again, your squares are the first I put grain into.

Paddy collects the tax at 90%: Reina pays 27 on Province 7's +30, the only positive income. The crown goes from -30 to -3, still in debt. Nothing is built and no new land can be bought this year, since a crown in debt can't pay a share of any work or square. Graham's salary is deferred.

The Jar goes up at eight. Reina, it's the one piece you need that nobody else at this table can use, and you've got the grain. I'm passing on the Brush. I'll bid on what the Pile has, and I won't pretend I'm not.
The Dragon Jar is needed by Reina (Wheat) and also by Paddy (Rice), who sold his to Graham. The Vase is needed by Graham and Paddy; the Land Deed Scroll by Graham; the Bamboo Brush by Reina.

The Jar's past my purse, and good luck to whoever takes it home. Reina, the Brush is on the block at two, like I promised; it's not quite my shelf any more, but it's waiting for you all the same. I'll have a go at the Vase with what I've got, and if Graham beats me to it a third time, I'll shake his hand, same as I did the first two.

Graham, that was clean, and I've been on the other end of a clean move before. I'll take the sixty and the wheat. The Jar comes to Province 7 at Graham's eight. Paddy, I'll take that Brush at two the way you promised, and I'll remember you kept the shelf for me. The Vase I'm not after, but Graham, don't count on getting it cheap.

The Jar and the Brush are going in the middle of the wheat, where everyone can see them. Paddy, you kept your word on the Brush, and I'll keep mine to you. Two down, Silke. I'm counting shelves this time, mine included.

The auctions. Reina takes Graham's Dragon Jar for 8 (his minimum; Graham keeps 2) and Paddy's Bamboo Brush for 2 (Paddy keeps 0.5), and puts them on Q15 and Q16. The Harvest Pile's Vase goes to Graham for 7: Paddy stopped at 4, Reina at 6. Graham takes the Land Deed Scroll for 2, uncontested. Grain: Silke -3 (the crown, in debt), Reina 23, Paddy 5, Graham 20.5.

That's the Bowl, the Brush, the Vase and the Scroll, and twenty in hand. Silke, I'm taking the throne. The crown's three short and I'll cover it; you draw sixty, which is more than the crown has had all year. Paddy, Reina: the tax will be what I can show you the numbers for.

Graham takes the throne with the Silk set (Bowl, Brush, Vase, Scroll) and 20.5 in hand. Every piece he held goes back to stock: the Vase and the Scroll to Province 7's (Reina's), the Bowl and the Brush to Province 6's (Paddy's), the Customs House to Province 5's. He takes the crown's -3, leaving him 17.5. Silke draws 60 and becomes the Silk Peasant, with Province 5. Grain: Graham (the crown) 17.5, Silke 60, Reina 23, Paddy 5.
Two projects are still owed, not one: the Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160).

Paddy, you keep the tax. You collected it honestly and you'll get two for it tonight. Reina, the bank and the I Ching are yours from next year, three a year each, and I'll pay it on time. Silke, you've sixty in hand, which is more than the crown has, so you'll forgive me for not paying you anything.

Graham hands out the jobs: Paddy keeps the tax; Reina banks the Harvest Pile and reads the I Ching from next year, at 3 a year for each job. He pays Paddy 2 for this year's collection. End of Year 7: Graham (the crown) 15.5, Silke 60, Reina 23, Paddy 7. Nobody is in debt. Beside the board: Province 5 (Silke) 1 Customs House; Province 6 (Paddy) 1 Wooden Bowl and 1 Bamboo Brush; Province 7 (Reina) 1 Vase and 1 Land Deed Scroll.

The Emperor's Share. 'The Emperor would like to remind you who paid for the ditch.' Every province gets an average harvest. Any province with a Public Works splits the extra harvest it brings in fifty-fifty with the Emperor this round, and that includes my Reservoir, which I seem to have paid for twice now. Population holds at three hundred million, times three, so read the x3 row, average column, and nobody plays a disaster. And Graham, I don't mean any disrespect, but the book says the card reader gets at least five, not three. I'll take five at the end of the year, the same as Silke paid it and I paid it.
An appointed reader's salary, like every appointee's at this table, is the Emperor's choice (Note 3); the 'at least 5' is a seated Scholar's due, and the reader's prompt overstated it.

Reina reads The Emperor's Share: an average harvest, no disasters, the population holds at x3. The harvest: Graham -5, Silke -5, Paddy +15, Reina +55. The Share: Province 7's Reservoir adds 20, so Reina pays Graham 10. Grain: Graham (the crown) 20.5, Silke 55, Reina 68, Paddy 22.

Thirty percent. That's twenty-one, and it's less than anyone here has paid under the last crown. Silke, one canal section in your province, twenty from you and twenty from me, and it's plus ten on your harvest every year after. Reina, it's three, as I said when I gave you the job. I don't pay more than I said, and I don't pay less.

Paddy collects the tax at 30%: Paddy 4.5, Reina 16.5, 21 to the crown, which now holds 41.5. Graham offers one section of the Grand Canal in Province 5 (40), split 20 from Silke and 20 from the crown, or nothing built this year; and 2 a square from the crown toward any province's new land, none for Province 1.

Graham, you're asking me to pay twenty for a canal that earns me ten a year, when twenty on a square of land earns me twenty. The canal is the crown's work, so build it with the crown's grain: I'll put in ten and you put in thirty. If not, leave it unbuilt, because every year that canal stays unbuilt is another year this game keeps going. I'll take two squares, K25 and K26, and I'm asking the crown for ten on each. Two a square isn't a subsidy, it's a tip. I ran this crown with an empty chest and still paid five a square, and you're sitting on forty-one. Everyone here can do that sum.

One square, Graham, Q26, right next to the paddies. I'll put in fifteen of my seventeen and a half and ask the crown for five, the same five a square Silke paid when the chest was empty. I'm not asking for a tip or a gift, just what the last crown managed.

No land for the wheat this year. Province 7 already pays fifty-five, and I'd rather the crown's grain go to the people who need it to break even. Graham, Paddy's asking for five a square, the same five Silke found with an empty chest, so give it to him. And three for the cards is your call, so I'll take it and say thank you.

Five a square, for everyone, which is what the last crown paid and what Paddy asked for. Silke, when I bought those four squares of wheat land I asked for one a square so you could still pay me, so I won't be told about tips. The canal waits until somebody thinks it's worth more than ten of their grain.

No work is built this year. New land at 5 a square from the crown: Silke buys K25 and K26 (she pays 30, the crown 10) and Paddy buys Q26 (he pays 15, the crown 5). Grain: Graham (the crown) 26.5, Silke 25, Reina 51.5, Paddy 2.5.

The Wooden Bowl goes up this year, starting at six. It's a good bowl, Graham paid nine for its brother once, and I'd rather it went to somebody who'll finish something with it than have it sit on my shelf. The Brush can wait a year. Thank you for the five a square, Graham. That square of rice will pay you back in tax.
The Scroll goes up at six. That's what Graham took it to me for once, so it's a fair price with some history to it. The Vase waits a year. It's been sold and resold enough for one table.

My Customs House goes at two. I don't need it, and I'm not going to bleed anyone for a piece they can't finish a set with. Reina, you and I both want that Bowl. You have the Jar and the Brush and twice my grain, so if you take it, everyone at this table can see how close you are to the throne. Remember, three quarters of every grain we spend bidding against each other goes into the Pile, so I won't chase you past what it's worth to me.

Reina is the Wheat Peasant: a complete Wheat set (Customs House, Bowl, Brush, Jar) lets her replace Silke or Paddy, not the Emperor. At this table only the Silk Peasant may take the throne with a set.

Two and a half grain doesn't bid on much, so I'm sitting this one out and watching. The Bowl's at six, like I said. Reina, Silke, if you both want it, settle it between you rather than feeding the Pile; it's all the same to me who carries it home, as long as somebody does.

Silke, you're right, and I won't pretend otherwise: if I take the Bowl, I'm one claim away from a seat. So here's my offer in public. Stand aside on the Bowl and the Scroll goes at two tonight instead of six, and the Vase goes up at two next year, with nothing from me against you on either. You'd be two pieces closer to the crown for four grain, and the Pile doesn't get fat on our quarrel. If you'd rather fight me for it, I have the grain to win.

The auctions. Reina takes Silke's Customs House for 2, uncontested, and Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 14 (Silke stopped at 13), and sets them on Q17 and Q18. Silke takes Reina's Land Deed Scroll at its minimum of 6. Reina's shelf now holds the full Wheat set: Customs House, Bowl, Brush and Jar.

The Scroll goes on P22, where my Vase used to sit. Reina, I should have taken your deal, and I'll say so in front of everyone. But you've just finished a set that can unseat me or Paddy, and not Graham, so think about who that really helps. If you come for the coast, the crown gets two grateful peasants at your expense. Leave me be, and next year the Vase at two is all I'm asking from you.

Silke, you said yourself that everyone at this table could see how close I was. I'm taking the Silk seat back, the coast I started from. You draw sixty and you get the wheat, the Reservoir I built, four good squares and fifty-five a year, which is better land than I'm getting. Graham, the coast is mine again, and you know what the Silk seat is for. The tax will be what you can show us the numbers for, just as you said.

Reina replaces Silke as the Silk Peasant (Province 5). She takes Silke's 19.5, leaving her 56.5. The Dragon Jar goes back to Province 5's stock; her Customs House, Bowl and Brush move to P23, P24 and P25. Silke returns the Land Deed Scroll to stock (Province 7's), draws 60 and becomes the Wheat Peasant, with Province 7 (the Reservoir and four squares). Reina keeps the bank and the I Ching. Grain: Graham (the crown) 26.5, Reina 56.5, Silke 60, Paddy 6. Beside the board: Province 5 (Reina) 1 Dragon Jar; Province 6 (Paddy) 1 Bamboo Brush; Province 7 (Silke) 1 Vase and 1 Land Deed Scroll.

Reina, six, as I promised. I don't change the price after the work's done. Next year the cards go to Paddy and the bank goes to Silke, three a job, and Paddy keeps the tax. Silke, the Vase and the Scroll are on your shelf now. Set your minimums the way you'd want them set if you were sitting in this chair.

Graham pays Reina 6 for the bank and the I Ching and Paddy 3 for the tax. Next year Paddy collects the tax and reads the I Ching, and Silke banks the Harvest Pile, at 3 a job. End of Year 8: Graham (the crown) 17.5, Reina 62.5, Silke 60, Paddy 9. Nobody is in debt. Seats: Graham Emperor (Province 1), Reina Silk Peasant (5), Paddy Rice Peasant (6), Silke Wheat Peasant (7). On the board: Reina's Customs House, Bowl and Brush (P23-P25); Paddy's Scroll and Customs House (R23, R24). Beside the board: Province 5 (Reina) 1 Dragon Jar; Province 6 (Paddy) 1 Bamboo Brush; Province 7 (Silke) 1 Vase and 1 Land Deed Scroll. New land: K25, K26 (Province 5) and Q26 (Province 6), yielding from next year. 320 of the works still owed: the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
The Silk set is the Wooden Bowl, Bamboo Brush, Vase and Land Deed Scroll: Reina holds two of the four (the Bowl and the Brush) and lacks the Vase and the Scroll.
The Silk set is the Wooden Bowl, Bamboo Brush, Vase and Land Deed Scroll: Reina holds two of the four (the Bowl and the Brush) and lacks the Vase and the Scroll.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." Population stays at three hundred million, so that's times three, everybody. Read the bad-harvest row at x3. Third rotten year I've turned up for this table, and I'm sorry, I'd have dealt you a better one if the cards let me.
This is the table's third bad harvest (Years 4, 7 and 9), and Paddy's first reading. An appointed reader's salary is the Emperor's choice; the 'at least 5' is a seated Scholar's due.

Paddy turns the eighth I Ching card: Bad Harvest. A bad harvest for every province, and no disasters. The population holds at 300 million, x3. This year's incomes: Graham -30, Reina +10, Paddy +10, Silke +30. The crown holds 17.5 and no realia, so the harvest would leave it at -12.5, in debt. Before the harvest is paid out, the table may give or lend grain.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

No need to apologise, Paddy, you read the card you were dealt. Here's the year: the crown has seventeen and a half and owes thirty, so after the harvest it's twelve and a half in debt. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's squares, and with three hundred million to feed, all of you will need squares. Reina, lend the crown thirteen now and I'll pay you back fifteen out of next year's tax. I paid you exactly what I promised last year, and I'll do it again. Silke, if Reina won't, the same terms go to you.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

Graham, you paid me what you promised and I haven't forgotten it. But every grain I have is already spoken for this year, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise and then come up short at the auction. If Silke wants your terms, they're fair terms. I'm just not the one who can take them this time.
The Emperor never bids at auction, whether the crown is in debt or not.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

Thirteen it is, Graham, and fifteen back next year. I asked you for thirty once and you said no, so I'm being kinder than you were. One condition, out loud so everyone hears it: a crown that isn't in debt doesn't need ninety percent. I know, because I'm the last one who charged it. Keep the tax decent and we're square.

Silke lends the crown 13 before the harvest, on Graham's terms: 15 back from next year's tax. Silke pays out the harvest: Graham -30, Reina +10, Paddy +10, Silke +30. Grain: Graham (the crown) 0.5, Reina 72.5, Silke 77, Paddy 19. Nobody is in debt.
Graham's promise for the tax and the I Ching is 3 a year for each job.

Thirty percent, Silke, same as last year, nothing like ninety: fifteen grain. Here's the chest: fifteen and a half in, nine out in salaries, three each to Paddy for the tax and the I Ching and to Silke for the bank, and that leaves six and a half. Reina, the canal in your province: thirty-six from you and four from the crown, and it adds ten to your harvest every year from now on. After that the crown pays one a square on your new land. It's not much, but it's what the numbers allow, and the crown stays out of debt so it can pay Silke her fifteen.

Graham taxes 30%: Reina 3, Paddy 3, Silke 9, collected by Paddy; the crown 15.5. His offers for the works step: one section of the Grand Canal in Province 5 (40), Reina 36 and the crown 4, or nothing built this year; and 1 a square from the crown on new land bought by any province this year, for two squares at most in all.

Graham, thank you, and I mean that. I've been asking for that canal since Year 5. But a canal that's thirty-six of mine and four of the crown's isn't the crown's canal, it's my canal with your name on it. Build it when the crown can carry it, and I'll cheer from the coast. Meanwhile I'm keeping my grain on the coast too.
Reina declines the canal split and buys no land, so on Graham's terms no work is built this year.

Graham, I've sixteen grain to my name, and the square's twenty. Your one a square won't get me there, so I'm asking four of you, and I'll put in every grain I've got. If the crown can't do four, I'll buy nothing and say no more about it. Times six is still in the deck, and I'd sooner meet it with one more field than with an empty bowl.
Paddy asks for one square of sea, Q27: he pays 16 and asks the crown for 4.
One square, Graham: nineteen from me and your one. That leaves your other square for Paddy, so the crown can decide whether it stretches to four for him. And don't spend my fifteen doing it.
Silke asks for one square of the Warlord's land, U14: she pays 19 and takes the crown's 1.

Paddy, four it is. Here's the count so everyone can check it: fifteen and a half in the chest, nine out in salaries, one for Silke's square and four for yours, and the crown ends the year on one and a half. That's not a grain in debt, Silke, and your fifteen comes out of next year's tax, as agreed. Reina, the canal offer stays open whenever you want it.

No work is built this year. New land: Paddy buys Q27 (sea) for 20, paying 16 with the crown's 4; Silke buys U14 (the Warlord's land) for 20, paying 19 with the crown's 1. Each yields 20 from next year. Grain: Graham (the crown) 10.5, Reina 69.5, Silke 49, Paddy 0. The crown has said it pays 9 in salaries at the year's end.

The auctions: each seller puts up one piece. Reina and Paddy each hold one type, so the Dragon Jar and the Bamboo Brush go up. Province 7's Vase was held back last year, and a piece may be held back one round, never two in a row, so the Vase goes up this year and the Land Deed Scroll waits. Each seller sets their own lot's minimum (at least 2) in their bids.

My Jar goes up at two, the honest price. Silke, you know what I'm after: the Vase is coming back to the coast where it started, and I'll pay a fair price for it in front of everyone. I'd much rather do that than run you up and feed the Pile.
I've an empty purse and a new field, so I'm sitting this one out. The Brush is up at two for anybody who wants it, and I'll not be bidding against anyone tonight.

Paddy's chest is empty and Graham's minding the crown's, so I'll say it plainly: I'm bidding on the Jar and the Brush, and I'm not getting into a war over either. The Vase goes up at two. Whoever wants it can have it cheap.
The Emperor never bids at auction.
Silke still needs four pieces for her set: a Customs House, a Bamboo Brush, the Dragon Jar and the Wooden Bowl.

The auctions. Reina's Dragon Jar goes to Silke for 2, her minimum, uncontested (Reina keeps 0.5). Paddy's Bamboo Brush goes to Reina for 16: Silke stopped at 15, and Reina bid only to keep it from Silke (Paddy keeps 4). Silke's Vase goes to Reina for 2, her minimum, uncontested (Silke keeps 0.5). The Land Deed Scroll stays in Province 7's stock. Grain: Reina 52, Silke 47.5, Paddy 4, Graham (the crown) 10.5.

Sixteen grain for a brush you'll never use, Reina, just so I can't have it. Twelve of that went into the pile. Keep spending like that and you'll win the argument and lose the coast. Thank you for the Jar, though.

Silke, two for the Vase, and that's generous of you, I won't forget it. The Brush I paid for in fear, sixteen grain against a shelf I counted wrong. Fair enough, Paddy, it went into your pocket and not into the river. That leaves one Scroll and twenty grain, and everyone here knows where the Scroll is.
A seller keeps a quarter of the price: of Reina's 16 for the Brush, Paddy keeps 4 and 12 goes to the Harvest Pile.

Graham pays Paddy 6 for the tax and the I Ching, and Silke 3 for the bank. End of Year 9: Graham (the crown) 1.5, owing Silke 15 from next year's tax; Reina 52, Silke 50.5, Paddy 10. Nobody is in debt. Reina holds the Customs House, the Bowl, two Brushes and the Vase, and needs only the Land Deed Scroll, the last piece in Province 7's stock. Silke holds the Dragon Jar. Land: 18 squares.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

Heaven Has Favourites. Some fields shine, some fields sulk." Provinces 2, 4 and 5 get a good harvest. Provinces 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8 get a bad one. Population stays at three hundred million, times three, so read the x3 row. Well, Reina, the sun's on the silk this year and the rain's on the rest of us. Graham, that's your north under the Wall gone sulky too, so I'd look to your bowl before you look to anybody's square.

Heaven Has Favourites: a good harvest for Province 5 and a bad one for Provinces 1, 6 and 7. The population holds at 300 million, x3, and nobody plays a disaster. This year's incomes: Graham -30, Reina +60, Paddy +30, Silke +50. The crown holds 1.5 and no realia, so the harvest would leave it at -28.5, in debt. Before the harvest is paid out, the table may give or lend grain.
An appointed reader's salary is the Emperor's choice; the 'at least 5' is a seated Scholar's due.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

The crown holds one and a half, and the north is down thirty, so I'll ask for exactly what it needs: twenty-nine before the harvest, thirty-three back out of next year's tax, after Silke's fifteen. Reina, you're the one province Heaven smiled on, so I'm asking you first, and in front of everyone. A crown in debt can't put a grain into anyone's field at the next population card, and that includes yours.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

Twenty-nine it is, Graham, and on your terms: thirty-three back after Silke's fifteen. I said in Year 7 that a crown in debt is bad for every field in China, and I'm not going to argue the other side of it now because the sun happens to be on my silk. Everyone heard the terms, so everyone can count them.

Reina lends the crown 29 before the harvest, on Graham's terms: 33 back from the crown's tax, after Silke's 15. Grain: Graham (the crown) 30.5, Reina 23. The harvest will leave the crown at 0.5, out of debt.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

Well lent, Reina. That's the crown out of the red, with my fifteen first in line, everyone heard it. I'll keep my grain in the sack this year. Somebody at this table has to have some left when the population card comes round.
Silke pays out the harvest. Grain: Graham (the crown) 0.5, Reina 83, Paddy 40, Silke 100.5. Nobody is in debt. The crown owes Silke 15 and Reina 33 from its tax.

Forty percent, and here's every grain of it. Fifty-six comes in. Fifteen goes to Silke and thirty-three to Reina, both in full, today, which leaves eight and a half. Nothing gets built this year because I won't start a forty-grain work on money I've already promised away, and I'll pay one a square on anyone's new land.

Graham taxes at 40%: Reina 24, Paddy 12, Silke 20, 56 in all. He repays both loans in full from it, 15 to Silke and 33 to Reina. Grain: Graham (the crown) 8.5, Reina 92, Paddy 28, Silke 95.5. Nothing is built this year. The crown pays 1 a square on new land bought by any other province, and buys none for Province 1.

One square of sea at N28, Graham, nineteen from me and your one from the crown, as you offered. I'm not going to stand here with ninety grain and let the coast go hungry, but I'm not going to pave it either, because there's a Scroll still to come this year.
New land: Reina buys N28 (sea) for 20, paying 19 with the crown's 1. Grain: Graham (the crown) 7.5, Reina 73.

Same as Reina, Graham: one square of sea at R27, nineteen from me and your one from the crown. I've twenty-eight grain, and I'd sooner it went into a field that feeds the south-east than sat in a sack while the two of you bid over a Scroll I can't use.
New land: Paddy buys R27 (sea) for 20, paying 19 with the crown's 1. Grain: Graham (the crown) 6.5, Paddy 9.

Two squares for the wheat, Graham, U15 and U16, nineteen each from me and your one a square, as you offered. The rain sulked on Province 7 this year, so I'm digging deeper before the next population card arrives, not after.
New land: Silke buys U15 and U16 (the Warlord's land) for 40, paying 38 with the crown's 2. Nothing is built this year. Land: 22 squares. Grain: Graham (the crown) 4.5, Reina 73, Silke 57.5, Paddy 9.

The auctions. Provinces 5 and 6 have no stock left, and the Harvest Pile holds none. Province 7's Land Deed Scroll was held back last year, so it must go up this year; Silke sets its minimum in her bids. The Emperor doesn't bid.
Everyone knows what this one is for, so I won't pretend otherwise. Silke, set your price where you like. I've kept my twenty for the claim, and whatever's left over that is yours to name.

I've nine grain and a Scroll already on my paddies, so I'll not push the price up on a piece I can't use. Bidding just to feed the Pile isn't my way. Reina, if it's yours, you'll have got it fair, and I'll say so.

You told me to name my price, Reina, so here it is: fifty-three. That leaves you exactly the twenty for your claim and not a grain over. You said in Year 8 you'd never forget the Vase at two. This is me remembering it for you.

The auction: Silke's Land Deed Scroll goes to Reina at Silke's minimum of 53, uncontested. Silke keeps a quarter, 13; 40 goes to the Harvest Pile. Grain: Reina 20, Silke 70.5, Paddy 9, Graham (the crown) 4.5. Reina now holds the Customs House, the Bowl, two Brushes, the Vase and the Scroll: a complete Silk set, with 20 in hand.

Fifty-three, Silke, and that's fair: you priced it to the grain, and I'd have done exactly the same. Graham, the Silk seat is yours again, and so is the coast I just put a new square on, so you won't be taking over an empty sack. The crown's coming back to where it started, and the first thing it does is pay its appointees and look north.

Reina takes the throne with the Silk set and 20 in hand. Every piece she held goes back to stock: the Customs House to Province 5's, the Bowl and both Brushes to Province 6's, the Vase and the Scroll to Province 7's. She takes the crown's 4.5: 24.5. Graham draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and becomes the Silk Peasant, with Province 5. Grain: Reina (the crown) 24.5, Graham 60, Silke 70.5, Paddy 9.

The crown pays what the crown promised, even when the promise was Graham's: six to Paddy and three to Silke. Same hands on the same jobs next year at the same three a job, because nothing worked last year that needs fixing. Paddy, I've known a crown that would give you nothing for reading a card. I wasn't that crown before and I'm not going to be now.

Reina pays Paddy 6 for the tax and the I Ching, and Silke 3 for the bank, and keeps the jobs where they are for next year at 3 a job. End of Year 10: Reina (the crown) 15.5, Graham 60, Silke 73.5, Paddy 15. Nobody is in debt. Land: 22 squares. Nothing built; the Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160) are still owed. Paddy holds a Scroll and a Customs House; Silke holds the Dragon Jar.
